name: Gift Wrap
description: Master the Gift Wrap setup from Mount in BJJ. Complete guide to arm isolation technique trapping opponent's arm across their body for back takes and submissions.
summary: The Gift Wrap from Mount is an arm-trapping transition where the top player threads an arm under the opponent's armpit and pins it high across their chest, stripping half their defense and opening back takes, chokes, and armbars.
overview:
Within the mount attack hierarchy, the Gift Wrap occupies the rung between raw positional control and direct submission, refining Mount's dominance into systematic limb isolation. By stripping away half of the opponent's defensive capability in a single action, it converts the already dominant mount into a submission-rich control configuration. The technique derives its name from the visual appearance of the trapped arm being 'wrapped' like a present across the defender's chest.

Strategically, the Gift Wrap serves as a critical transitional hub within the mount attack system. Once the arm is trapped across the opponent's chest toward their opposite shoulder, multiple high-percentage attack paths become available: the rear naked choke becomes substantially easier due to reduced hand fighting, back control transitions open as the opponent is forced to turn away, and the free arm becomes an isolated target for armbar attacks. The Gift Wrap exemplifies modern positional methodology where control is refined before submission attempts.

The key to successful Gift Wrap entries lies in understanding opponent reactions. When you threaten submissions from mount—armbars, collar chokes, or Ezekiels—the opponent naturally extends or repositions their arms defensively. These defensive movements create the arm isolation opportunities that facilitate the Gift Wrap entry. Patient practitioners who set up the wrap through positional pressure and submission threats achieve significantly higher success rates than those who attempt to force the arm across.
conditions: Mount position established with solid base and weight distribution
At least one of opponent's arms is isolated or positioned away from their centerline
Opponent is actively defending submissions, creating arm exposure opportunities
Chest-to-chest pressure maintained throughout setup phase

attacker.name: Gift Wrap Attacker
attacker.description: How to execute Gift Wrap in BJJ. Attacking perspective with setup, execution steps, and counters.
attacker.overview:
The Gift Wrap is a fundamental arm-trapping transition executed from Mount that establishes dominant control by wrapping one of the opponent's arms across their own body and securing it with your grip. This technique systematically removes half of the opponent's defensive capability in a single action, transforming the already dominant mount position into a submission-rich control configuration. The position derives its name from the visual appearance of the trapped arm being 'wrapped' like a present across the defender's chest.

Strategically, the Gift Wrap serves as a critical transitional hub within the mount attack system. Once the arm is trapped across the opponent's chest toward their opposite shoulder, multiple high-percentage attack paths become available: the rear naked choke becomes substantially easier due to reduced hand fighting, back control transitions open as the opponent is forced to turn away, and the free arm becomes an isolated target for armbar attacks. The Gift Wrap exemplifies modern positional methodology where control is refined before submission attempts.

The key to successful Gift Wrap entries lies in understanding opponent reactions. When you threaten submissions from mount—armbars, collar chokes, or Ezekiels—the opponent naturally extends or repositions their arms defensively. These defensive movements create the arm isolation opportunities that facilitate the Gift Wrap entry. Patient practitioners who set up the wrap through positional pressure and submission threats achieve significantly higher success rates than those who attempt to force the arm across.
key_principles: Isolate the target arm before attempting to wrap—chasing the arm without isolation leads to failure
Thread your controlling arm under opponent's armpit from outside to inside for maximum mechanical advantage
Pull trapped arm high across opponent's chest toward opposite shoulder—high positioning prevents recovery
Maintain mount fundamentals throughout—knees tight, weight forward, hips heavy
Use submission feints to create arm isolation opportunities rather than forcing the wrap
The Gift Wrap is transitional control, not an endpoint—immediately threaten to prevent defensive reset
setup_requirements: Mount position established with solid base and weight distribution
Opponent's arm has become isolated through defensive movement or your submission feints
At least one of opponent's arms is positioned away from their centerline
Your chest maintains pressure on opponent's upper body throughout setup
Opponent is defending submissions with one arm extended or positioned across body

execution_steps.description: From Mount, identify which arm is most isolated or exposed through opponent's defensive positioning. Look for the arm that is furthest from centerline or being used to push against your hips or chest defensively.

Secure grip control on the target arm's wrist or lower forearm using your same-side hand. This initial grip prevents the opponent from retracting the arm while you establish the threading position for the wrap.

Drive your opposite arm under the opponent's armpit from the outside, reaching diagonally across their chest toward the trapped wrist. Your arm travels from their armpit toward their opposite shoulder area, creating the wrap configuration.

Transfer wrist control to your threading arm by gripping opponent's wrist or forearm with the hand that traveled under their armpit. Your original controlling hand is now free to establish secondary control or head control.

Pull the trapped arm high across the opponent's chest toward their opposite shoulder using your threading arm. The higher the arm positioning, the more difficult recovery becomes for the opponent. Maintain constant upward pulling pressure.

Use your free hand to control opponent's head, underhook their neck, or reinforce the arm trap. This secondary control prevents the rotation they need to recover the trapped arm. Your chest drives forward onto their wrapped arm.

Settle your weight, ensure the trapped arm remains high across their chest, and verify your mount base remains intact. The Gift Wrap is now established as a platform for back takes, submissions, or positional advancement.

common_counters.counter: Opponent retracts arm before wrap is established by pulling elbow tight to ribs and keeping arm close to centerline
common_counters.your_response: Feint toward collar choke or Ezekiel to force defensive arm extension, then immediately attack the Gift Wrap entry on their extended defending arm

common_counters.counter: Opponent bridges explosively during the arm threading to disrupt your base and create space
common_counters.your_response: Post with free hand toward their head, drive hips down to absorb bridge, and use their settling movement to complete threading before they can bridge again

common_counters.counter: Opponent rotates shoulder forward aggressively to slip out of the developing wrap before it locks
common_counters.your_response: Keep constant pulling pressure on trapped wrist while driving chest forward—their rotation should actually help bring the arm across their body

common_counters.counter: Opponent uses free hand to grip-fight your threading arm and prevent wrap completion
common_counters.your_response: Their free hand interference exposes their neck—threaten collar choke or Ezekiel forcing them to use both hands for defense, then re-attack Gift Wrap

common_counters.counter: Opponent hip escapes during threading phase to insert knee and recover half guard
common_counters.your_response: Drive your knee back across their thigh to re-center your mount before the escape completes, or abandon the wrap and address the positional threat first

common_errors.error: Attempting to force the wrap without first isolating the target arm through setup or feints
common_errors.consequence: Opponent easily retracts arm and you waste energy while potentially compromising mount stability
common_errors.correction: Wait for or create arm isolation through submission feints before attempting the wrap—patience in setup is essential for success

common_errors.error: Threading arm too shallow without reaching deep enough across to the opposite side
common_errors.consequence: Trap has no holding power and opponent easily extracts arm through shoulder rotation
common_errors.correction: Reach deep under armpit with threading arm, ensuring you can grip wrist or forearm on the far side of their chest

common_errors.error: Allowing trapped arm to slide low toward opponent's hip or waist area
common_errors.consequence: Creates space for opponent to rotate shoulder and recover arm, losing all accumulated trap advantage
common_errors.correction: Keep constant upward pulling pressure on trapped arm toward their opposite shoulder—high positioning equals tight control

common_errors.error: Rising up and losing chest-to-chest pressure during the transition phase
common_errors.consequence: Creates bridging space and may allow opponent to insert frames or begin guard recovery
common_errors.correction: Maintain forward weight distribution throughout—your chest should continue pressuring their chest even while threading

common_errors.error: Neglecting mount maintenance fundamentals while focusing entirely on arm trap
common_errors.consequence: Opponent escapes mount during transition, wasting the position for a failed control attempt
common_errors.correction: Gift Wrap is an enhancement to mount control, not a replacement—knees must stay tight, weight forward, hips heavy

common_errors.error: Grip transferring too slowly between initial wrist control and threading arm
common_errors.consequence: Opponent senses the momentary looseness during grip transfer and retracts arm to centerline before wrap locks
common_errors.correction: Drill grip transfer as a single fluid motion—the threading hand must contact opponent's wrist before releasing the initial controlling hand

training_progressions.description: Practice the arm threading motion with cooperative partner. Focus on the path from outside the armpit to gripping the opposite wrist. Drill grip transfers between hands. Partner offers no resistance, allowing focus on proper mechanics.

Add light resistance as partner attempts minor bridging and arm recovery. Focus on maintaining mount control while executing the transition. Practice recovering when wrap fails and immediately re-attempting.

Partner defends realistically. Practice creating Gift Wrap entries through submission feints—threaten collar choke or armbar to force defensive arm positioning that facilitates the wrap. Chain failed entries into immediate re-attacks.

Full resistance positional sparring starting from Mount. Execute Gift Wrap against realistic defense and immediately chain to follow-up attacks (back take, armbar, chokes). Track success rate and identify technique gaps.

flashcards.question: What is the primary goal of the Gift Wrap transition from Mount?
flashcards.answer: The primary goal is to trap one of the opponent's arms across their own body, eliminating half of their defensive capability. This creates a dominant control position that serves as a gateway to back takes, rear naked chokes, and armbars on the free arm. The Gift Wrap transforms Mount into a systematic attack platform where defensive options are progressively eliminated.
flashcards.answer_line: Trap one arm across their body

plausible: Control both wrists tightly
Go straight for a choke
trap: Abandon mount to chase the arm

flashcards.question: What is the optimal height to maintain the trapped arm across the opponent's body?
flashcards.answer: The trapped arm should be pulled high across the opponent's chest toward their opposite shoulder. This high positioning prevents arm recovery through shoulder rotation and maintains maximum control effectiveness. If the arm drifts too low toward the hip or waist, the opponent gains mechanical advantage to extract the arm through rotational movements.

plausible: High, toward the near shoulder
Mid-chest height is sufficient
trap: Let it rest near the waist

flashcards.question: Your opponent keeps both arms tight to their body from mount bottom—how do you create the Gift Wrap entry?
flashcards.answer: Use submission feints to force defensive arm extension. Attack an Ezekiel choke, collar choke, or americana—any threat that forces them to use their arms defensively. As they push on your attacking arm or extend to create frames, immediately abandon the submission attempt and attack the exposed arm for the Gift Wrap entry. Their defensive reaction creates the arm isolation you need.
flashcards.answer_line: Feint a submission to bait extension

plausible: Pry the arms apart by force
Wait for them to move first
trap: Lunge for the arm and get rolled

flashcards.question: What is the critical relationship between mount control and the Gift Wrap transition?
flashcards.answer: Mount control must be maintained throughout the transition—the Gift Wrap is an enhancement to mount, not a replacement for it. Your knees must stay tight, your weight must stay forward, and your hips must stay heavy. If you neglect mount fundamentals while focusing on the arm trap, you risk losing the entire position. Establish solid mount first, then add the arm trap while maintaining all mount control principles.

plausible: Prioritize the arm trap first
Loosen your knees to reach the arm
trap: Sit up to free the trapping arm

flashcards.question: Your threading arm is in position but opponent is grip-fighting your wrist control—what adjustment do you make?
flashcards.answer: Their grip fighting on your wrist control hand is occupying their free arm. Threaten their exposed neck with your threading arm side—this forces a defensive priority shift. They must choose between continuing to fight your wrist grip or defending their neck. Either choice opens opportunity: if they release your wrist to defend neck, complete the wrap immediately; if they continue grip fighting, attack the neck.
flashcards.answer_line: Threaten the neck to force a choice

plausible: Rip the wrist free with strength
Switch straight to an armbar
trap: Release the wrist grip to reset

flashcards.question: How do you respond when the opponent bridges explosively during the Gift Wrap entry?
flashcards.answer: Post your free hand wide toward their head to create a stable tripod base while driving your hips down into their chest. The key is anticipating the bridge and loading your weight forward before they complete the explosive movement. If already committed to threading, continue the wrap—your forward pressure should absorb their bridge. Use their settling movement after the bridge fails to complete the arm trap.

plausible: Sit back to absorb the bridge
Abandon the wrap, regain grips
trap: Post hands narrow on their chest

flashcards.question: After establishing Gift Wrap, your opponent begins turning toward you—how do you capitalize?
flashcards.answer: Their turn toward you is an opportunity rather than an escape. Follow their rotation while maintaining the Gift Wrap arm control and transition to Technical Mount or back control. Use your hooks to guide their rotation rather than fighting it. The arm trap remains intact throughout, and you end in an even more dominant position. Flow with their movement to advance position.

plausible: Stop the turn and reset mount
Release the arm to block the turn
trap: Back off and let them recover guard

flashcards.question: What creates the mechanical leverage to thread your arm across a resistant opponent's body?
flashcards.answer: First control their wrist to prevent retraction, then use your chest weight pressing down on their upper arm and shoulder to pin their elbow. This creates a lever where the pinned elbow is the fulcrum. Without this elbow pressure, you're trying to muscle their entire arm across. With elbow controlled, you only need to guide their forearm, requiring far less force.
flashcards.answer_line: Pin the elbow with chest weight

plausible: Pull the wrist with both hands
Push down on their shoulder blade
trap: Reach hard and get bridged over

flashcards.question: Your opponent straightens their arm explosively as you begin the wrap—what is the correct response?
flashcards.answer: Convert immediately to armbar attack. Their defensive straightening actually exposes the arm for submission. Do not chase the Gift Wrap against an extended arm—the straightening is a mistake that creates a better submission opportunity. Secure the extended wrist, control the elbow, and transition to the armbar appropriate for their arm angle. Take what the opponent gives you.

plausible: Isolate the elbow before attacking
Trap the wrist, then re-secure wrap
trap: Keep forcing the wrap, lose the back

flashcards.question: What determines when to attack Gift Wrap versus maintaining mount pressure?
flashcards.answer: Attack Gift Wrap when opponent creates arm isolation through defensive movement—when they push on your hips or chest, when they reach across their body, or when they defend submission attempts with extended arms. Maintain mount pressure when both of their arms are tucked tight to their body. Use submission threats to create the defensive reactions that expose arms for Gift Wrap entries.

plausible: Attack the instant mount is secured
Wait until back control is close
trap: Force the wrap against tucked arms

flashcards.question: What grip configuration provides the strongest Gift Wrap control during the consolidation phase?
flashcards.answer: The threading arm grips opponent's wrist or lower forearm on the far side of their chest, with the arm running diagonally under their armpit. Your free hand controls behind their head or cups the back of their neck, creating a clamp between the head control and the arm trap. This configuration prevents both arm recovery and the head turn needed to initiate escapes. The diagonal line of the threading arm is the structural backbone of the entire control.
flashcards.answer_line: Wrist grip diagonal, hand on neck

plausible: Grip the wrist, free hand on hip
Both hands grip the trapped wrist
trap: Let go of the head to hunt legs

attacker.safety_considerations: The Gift Wrap transition is generally low-risk when executed with proper technique. The primary safety concern is avoiding excessive force on the trapped arm, which could cause shoulder strain or rotator cuff injury. Pull the arm across the chest using positional pressure rather than cranking force. During training, communicate immediately if the shoulder position becomes uncomfortable—tap early rather than risking injury. Partners should release the trap immediately upon tap, as continued pressure on an isolated shoulder joint can cause lasting damage. Avoid explosive jerking movements when establishing the wrap; smooth, steady pressure is both more effective and safer for training partners.

defender.name: Gift Wrap Defender
defender.description: How to defend against Gift Wrap in BJJ. Recognition cues, defensive options, and escape strategies from mount bottom.
defender.overview:
Defending the Gift Wrap from mount bottom is one of the most time-sensitive defensive challenges in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. The Gift Wrap transition strips away half of your defensive tools by trapping one arm across your own body, so your defensive window is narrow and diminishes rapidly as the wrap consolidates. The critical insight for defenders is that prevention is far more effective than escape—once the arm is fully wrapped high across the chest with secondary head control established, recovery becomes extremely difficult.

The defender's strategy operates on a timeline of decreasing options. During the initial wrist control phase, the defender retains the most escape routes: retracting the arm, grip-fighting the controlling hand, or bridging to disrupt the attacker's base. As the threading progresses, options narrow to shoulder rotation and explosive arm recovery. Once the wrap is locked with arm pulled high, the defender must shift entirely to positional escape (hip escape to half guard recovery) rather than arm recovery, since the mechanical advantage heavily favors the attacker. Understanding where you are on this timeline dictates which defensive response is appropriate.

The defender must also recognize that the Gift Wrap is a gateway position—the attacker will use it to advance to back control, Technical Mount, or direct submission attacks. Defensive priorities therefore extend beyond simply freeing the arm: preventing the attacker from using the wrap to transition to an even worse position is equally important. Maintaining hip positioning, preventing the turn that leads to back exposure, and keeping frames active with the free arm are all concurrent defensive tasks that must be managed alongside arm recovery attempts.
key_principles: Prevention is the strongest defense—keep elbows tight to ribs and arms close to centerline to deny the initial arm isolation
Recognize the Gift Wrap attempt at the earliest possible stage (wrist control) when defensive options are most numerous
Free arm must prioritize neck defense over arm recovery when attacker threatens chokes from the Gift Wrap position
Hip escape creates the space needed for arm recovery—you cannot muscle the arm free without first creating positional space
Avoid turning away from the attacker, which exposes the back and converts Gift Wrap into back control
Time defensive explosions to the attacker's grip transfer moment, when control is momentarily weakest
recognition_cues: Attacker secures same-side wrist control on one of your arms while maintaining mount—this is the earliest warning of a Gift Wrap attempt
Attacker's opposite arm begins driving under your armpit from the outside, reaching across your chest diagonally toward the controlled wrist
You feel your arm being pulled across your own body toward the opposite shoulder while weight increases on your upper chest
Attacker's head drops forward and chest pressure increases as they commit weight to the threading motion
Your shoulder mobility on one side becomes progressively restricted as the wrap tightens and the arm is elevated across your chest

defensive_options.action: Retract arm explosively by pulling elbow tight to ribs and rotating shoulder inward before the threading arm connects
defensive_options.when_to_use: During the initial wrist control phase before the attacker has threaded their arm under your armpit—this is the highest-percentage window for prevention
defensive_options.if_successful: You deny the Gift Wrap entry entirely and return to standard mount defense with both arms available for framing and escape
defensive_options.risk: If the retraction fails and the attacker maintains wrist control, you have expended energy without escaping and the wrap continues

defensive_options.action: Bridge explosively toward the side of the trapped arm to disrupt the attacker's base and threading angle during the wrap attempt
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker commits weight forward during the threading motion—their forward lean creates vulnerability to lateral bridging
defensive_options.if_successful: The bridge disrupts the threading motion and may create enough space for arm retraction or a full mount escape to guard recovery
defensive_options.risk: Failed bridge wastes energy and the attacker may use the settling phase to complete the wrap while you are flat on your back

defensive_options.action: Hip escape toward the trapped arm side while framing with free arm on attacker's hip to create distance for knee insertion
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the Gift Wrap is partially or fully established and arm recovery is no longer viable—shift priority from arm recovery to positional escape
defensive_options.if_successful: You recover half guard with one arm still trapped but have regained leg entanglement that prevents further positional advancement
defensive_options.risk: The hip escape may expose your back if the attacker follows your hip movement and converts to back control during the escape

defensive_options.action: Two-on-one grip fight the attacker's threading wrist with your free hand while rotating trapped shoulder forward to strip the wrap
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker has threaded under the armpit but has not yet completed the grip transfer to lock the wrap—target the transitional grip moment
defensive_options.if_successful: You break the wrap at its weakest structural point and recover the trapped arm to restore full defensive capability from mount bottom
defensive_options.risk: Using your free hand for grip fighting removes it from neck defense, creating a momentary window for the attacker to attack the choke

favorable_outcomes.how: Deny the Gift Wrap entry entirely by retracting the targeted arm during the initial wrist control phase. Keep elbows pinched tight to ribs and immediately grip-fight any wrist control attempt. Time a strong bridge during the attacker's forward lean to disrupt threading. The goal is to return to standard mount bottom defense with both arms available.

When the Gift Wrap is partially or fully established and arm recovery is not immediately possible, shift to positional escape. Frame on the attacker's hip with your free arm, hip escape toward the trapped arm side, and insert your knee to recover half guard. Accept the trapped arm temporarily and focus on regaining leg entanglement that prevents back take or further advancement.

common_errors.error: Extending arms to push attacker away during mount, creating the arm isolation the Gift Wrap requires
common_errors.consequence: Your extended arm is exactly what the attacker needs—the push creates the distance between your arm and body that allows the threading motion to begin
common_errors.correction: Keep elbows pinched tight to your ribs at all times from mount bottom. Frame with forearms against the attacker's hips or cross-face area rather than pushing with extended arms. Defensive framing should be structural, not pushing.

common_errors.error: Fighting the arm trap with muscular effort after the wrap is fully locked rather than addressing the position
common_errors.consequence: Rapid energy depletion with no positional improvement—the attacker has superior mechanical advantage once the diagonal wrap is established across your chest
common_errors.correction: Once the wrap is locked, shift immediately to hip escape and positional recovery. Use body movement and shoulder rotation rather than arm strength to create recovery opportunities. Energy spent pulling against a locked wrap is wasted.

common_errors.error: Turning away from the attacker to escape the arm trap, exposing the back
common_errors.consequence: The Gift Wrap becomes a back take—the attacker follows your turn, inserts hooks, and transitions to back control while maintaining the arm trap throughout
common_errors.correction: Never turn away from an attacker who has Gift Wrap control. If you must turn, turn toward the attacker to reduce the wrap angle. Hip escape laterally without rotating your shoulders away from the attacker.

common_errors.error: Neglecting neck defense with free arm while attempting to recover the trapped arm
common_errors.consequence: Attacker immediately attacks rear naked choke or cross collar choke while your only available hand is occupied with arm recovery instead of protecting your neck
common_errors.correction: Free arm must maintain neck defense as primary responsibility. Use hip movement, shoulder rotation, and body positioning for arm recovery rather than committing your free hand to grip-fighting the trap.

common_errors.error: Lying flat on back without creating angle or hip escape movement after the wrap is established
common_errors.consequence: Attacker settles full weight, completes secondary head control, and systematically advances to back take or submission with no disruption to their attacking plan
common_errors.correction: Immediately begin hip escaping the moment you feel the arm being drawn across your chest. Even if the wrap succeeds, maintaining hip movement and angle prevents the attacker from settling and creates recovery windows.

flashcards.question: What is the earliest recognition cue that a Gift Wrap attempt is beginning from mount?
flashcards.answer: The earliest cue is the attacker securing same-side wrist control on one of your arms while in mount. This wrist control is the foundation of the entire Gift Wrap sequence—without it, the attacker cannot prevent arm retraction during the threading phase. Recognizing this grip as a Gift Wrap precursor rather than a generic mount control allows you to initiate your defensive response at the stage where you have the most options.

plausible: Attacker's hand near your collar
Attacker basing on your hips
trap: Wait until the arm is fully trapped

flashcards.question: Why is turning away from the attacker during a Gift Wrap the worst possible defensive response?
flashcards.answer: Turning away exposes your back directly to the attacker who already has one of your arms trapped. The Gift Wrap arm control translates seamlessly into back control—the attacker follows your rotation, inserts hooks, and arrives in back mount with the arm still trapped. This converts a bad position into a catastrophic one. Always turn toward the attacker if you must rotate, or hip escape laterally without rotating your shoulders.
flashcards.answer_line: It exposes your back to them

plausible: It only costs valuable time
It just gives up half guard
trap: It's fine if you turn quickly

flashcards.question: Your arm is fully wrapped and locked high across your chest—what is your immediate defensive priority?
flashcards.answer: Shift from arm recovery to positional escape. Once the wrap is locked with the arm high, the mechanical advantage prevents muscular extraction. Use your free arm to frame on the attacker's hip, begin hip escaping toward the trapped arm side, and work to insert your knee for half guard recovery. Accept the arm trap temporarily and focus on preventing further positional advancement while working toward guard recovery.

plausible: Keep yanking to free the arm
Bridge hard to buck them off

flashcards.question: When during the Gift Wrap sequence is the attacker's control at its weakest and most vulnerable to disruption?
flashcards.answer: The grip transfer moment—when the attacker releases their initial wrist control hand to let the threading arm take over the grip—represents the weakest link in the sequence. For a brief instant, neither hand has a secure locked grip on your wrist. Time an explosive arm retraction or bridge to this exact moment. Reading the grip transfer requires drilling against the technique repeatedly to develop the timing sensitivity.

plausible: The moment wrist control starts
Once back control is threatened

flashcards.question: How should you use your free arm when your opponent has partially established the Gift Wrap and is threatening your neck?
flashcards.answer: Your free arm must prioritize neck defense above all other tasks. Tuck your chin and use your free hand to create a defensive frame against the attacker's choking arm, gripping their wrist or forearm to prevent it from sliding under your chin. Do not use the free arm to attempt arm recovery when neck threats are active—losing the neck battle ends the match immediately, while the arm trap alone does not. Once the choke threat is neutralized, you can briefly redirect the free hand to assist positional escape.
flashcards.answer_line: Frame the neck, not the trapped arm

plausible: Split focus between neck and arm
Prioritize freeing the trapped arm
trap: Ignore the neck, escape the arm

training_progressions.description: Partner attempts Gift Wrap entries from mount at 30% speed. Defender focuses on recognizing the wrist control and threading cues as early as possible. Practice immediate arm retraction and elbow-pinch defense. Develop awareness of the Gift Wrap timeline and which defensive options exist at each stage.

Partner increases speed to 50-70%. Defender practices grip fighting the threading arm, timing bridges to the attacker's forward lean, and explosive arm retraction during the grip transfer moment. Drill the transition from arm defense to positional escape when the wrap succeeds.

Start each rep with the Gift Wrap already established. Defender practices hip escape to half guard recovery, free arm neck defense, and shoulder rotation for arm recovery. Partner threatens chokes and back takes to add realistic pressure. Develop ability to manage multiple threats simultaneously.

Full resistance rounds starting from mount with the attacker actively hunting the Gift Wrap. Defender uses complete defensive toolkit including prevention, active defense, and escape. Track how often the Gift Wrap is prevented versus established, and success rate of escapes when it is locked.

variants_and_adaptations.description: Attack Ezekiel choke or collar choke, forcing opponent to extend arm defensively. As they push on your choking arm, immediately abandon the choke and wrap their extended arm. Their defensive reaction creates the arm isolation needed.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: Against opponents who maintain tight defensive posture until directly threatened with submission

variants_and_adaptations.description: Use cross-face pressure with your free arm to turn opponent's head away, which naturally brings their defending arm across their body toward your threading arm. The cross-face creates arm positioning that facilitates the wrap.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent keeps arms tight and centered, making direct arm isolation difficult

variants_and_adaptations.description: Without gi grips available, use a wrist ride control where you pin their wrist to their chest with your forearm while establishing the wrap. Requires tighter body positioning due to lack of friction from no-gi conditions.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: No-gi grappling situations where standard gi-based controls are unavailable

position_integration: The Gift Wrap functions as a critical transitional hub within the mount attack system, connecting basic mount control to advanced submission chains and positional advancements. From Mount, it represents a high-percentage pathway to back control since the arm trap naturally facilitates transitions when opponents attempt to turn away. The technique chains directly to rear naked choke attacks (reduced hand fighting), armbar on the free arm (isolated limb), Technical Mount (maintaining arm control while improving position), and Crucifix (trapping the second arm during transitions). Understanding Gift Wrap as a control enhancement rather than a destination position allows practitioners to use it strategically throughout exchanges, creating dominant control points while systematically eliminating defensive options.
